results.derivation_summary: Under 12 C.F.R. § 1006.14(b)(2), a debt collector is presumed to comply with the harassment prohibition (and FDCPA § 806(5)) if it places no more than seven calls to a particular person about a particular debt within seven consecutive days, and does not call that person about that debt within seven consecutive days after having had a telephone conversation with them (the conversation date counts as day one of that seven-day window). Exceeding either limit creates a presumption of violation, subject to the exclusions in paragraph (b)(3). The limits are counted per 'particular debt,' meaning each separate debt in collection, except that student loans serviced under a single account number when obtained by the collector count as one debt (§ 1006.14(b)(4)). Note that state law may be stricter: Massachusetts' 940 CMR 7.04(1)(f) limits debt collectors to two telephone communications per seven-day period to a debtor's residence/personal or cellular number for each debt.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer speaks with the collector on Monday, can't pay that day, and says 'call me back Thursday after I get paid and I'll set something up.' The collector calls Thursday (day 4) with a payoff figure. The consumer later asks whether the Thursday call violated the call-frequency rules.
edge_cases.gap_description: The encoded 'determination' makes any call within 7 days of a telephone conversation presumptively unlawful with no carve-out, while the consent exclusion is filed only under 'exclusions_from_count' (i.e., appears to apply only to the >7 raw count). Under 12 CFR 1006.14(b)(3), the exclusions apply to BOTH (b)(2)(i) and (b)(2)(ii), so a call placed with the consumer's prior consent given directly to the collector during the 7-day window is excluded from the post-conversation cooldown as well. Consumer-requested callbacks are extremely common, and the node as written would tell such a consumer she has a presumptive violation when she does not.

edge_cases.scenario: A collector dials the consumer's cell 14 times in six days about one debt. The consumer never picks up and the collector never leaves a message; the phone simply rings and goes unanswered or to an untouched voicemail box. The consumer asks whether the 7-in-7 rule was broken.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node lists 'calls not connected to the dialed number' as an exclusion with no definition. Official commentary to 12 CFR 1006.14(b)(3)(ii) limits that exclusion to calls that never connect (e.g., dropped by the carrier, no service); a call that rings through unanswered or reaches voicemail IS connected and counts. Unanswered ringing is the single most common fact pattern in these cases, and the undefined exclusion invites the answer 'those calls don't count,' which would wrongly negate a clear presumptive violation.

edge_cases.scenario: A collector calls the consumer's mother six times in one week asking her to pass along a message about her daughter's overdue account. The consumer asks whether those calls are a problem.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node affirmatively states that a genuinely different person (expressly, 'the consumer's mother') gets her own separate 7-call bucket, which implies six calls to the mother are presumptively lawful. It never flags that FDCPA § 1692c(b)/12 CFR 1006.6(d) generally prohibit communicating with third parties about the debt at all, and that § 1692b/1006.10 limit location-information contacts to a single call absent a request. Relative-calling is a very common complaint, and the encoding would tell a consumer with a strong third-party-disclosure claim that the conduct sits inside a safe harbor.

results.derivation_summary: Under § 1692a(6), an entity is a 'debt collector' if it uses interstate commerce or the mails in a business whose principal purpose is collecting debts, or if it regularly collects (directly or indirectly) debts owed or asserted to be owed to another; a creditor collecting its own debts under a false name indicating a third party is also covered, and enforcers of security interests count only for § 1692f(6) purposes. Even if a prong is met, the entity is excluded if it fits (A)–(F), e.g., a creditor's own officers/employees collecting in the creditor's name, affiliated in-house collectors whose principal business is not collection, government officers, process servers, nonprofit credit counselors, or persons collecting debts they originated, that were not in default when obtained, or held under fiduciary/escrow or commercial secured-party arrangements. Henson holds that a company collecting debts it purchased for its own account is not thereby collecting debts 'owed another,' although the Court expressly left open whether such a debt buyer could still qualify under the separate 'principal purpose' definition (and § 1692a(4) excludes from 'creditor' anyone taking assignment of a defaulted debt solely to facilitate collection for another). The supplied text defines the FDCPA gate only; it says nothing about Regulation F's scope, so that part cannot be derived here.

edge_cases.scenario: A sole proprietor took out a $40,000 equipment loan and a guaranty on a commercial line of credit; after default the lender placed the accounts with an outside collection agency that now calls him 10 times a day at home and threatens to 'have him arrested.' He wants to know if the agency violated the FDCPA/Reg F call-frequency and false-threat rules.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node gates only on WHO the entity is and never on WHAT is being collected. The FDCPA applies only to a 'debt' as defined in 1692a(5) -- an obligation of a natural person arising from a transaction primarily for personal, family, or household purposes. Business/commercial debts (and, similarly, most government fines, tickets, tolls, and non-transactional obligations) are outside the Act entirely, no matter how squarely the collector fits 1692a(6). Applied as encoded, the checklist returns 'COVERED' for the small-business borrower and every downstream node (7-in-7, validation notice, false-practices catalog) would then be applied, telling him he has federal claims he does not have. There is also no consumer/'natural person' element in the checklist.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer's car is repossessed by a repossession company retained by the auto lender, and separately a law firm handling a nonjudicial foreclosure sends her statutory notices of sale. Neither sent a 1692g validation notice, and the repo agent shouted at her in the driveway; she asks whether they broke the FDCPA.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node has no treatment of security-interest enforcement. Under 1692a(6)'s final sentence, a person whose only 'debt collection' business is enforcing security interests is a debt collector solely for purposes of 1692f(6), and Obduskey v. McCarthy & Holthus (2019) holds a business engaged in no more than nonjudicial foreclosure is likewise covered only by 1692f(6). Applied as encoded, both entities are 'regularly collecting debts owed another' with no listed exclusion, so the node returns full COVERAGE and the consumer would be told the validation-notice, call-frequency and general unfair/deceptive nodes apply to them -- a materially wrong answer in both directions of a very common fact pattern (auto repossession and foreclosure).

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer is 45 days past due on a credit card. An outside vendor the bank hired for 'early-out' recovery begins calling, identifying itself as a collection agency, and misstates the balance. The card agreement says the account is in default the day a payment is missed, but the bank does not charge off or 'place' accounts until 120 days.
edge_cases.gap_description: Checklist item 3 asks a servicer/assignee whether it got the debt before or after 'default,' but the node never defines default (the FDCPA does not; courts look to the underlying contract or to charge-off/placement practice) and, more importantly, invites applying the (F)(iii) exclusion to a retained third-party collection agent. (F)(iii) shelters persons who 'obtained' the debt (ownership or servicing rights) not in default -- most courts do not use it to exempt a collection agency hired to work a delinquent account, and a dedicated collection agency is independently covered under the principal-purpose prong. As encoded, a user with a common early-out/pre-charge-off collector would likely be routed to 'excluded, no FDCPA claim,' a false negative on a live claim.

gaps_found.gap_description: Checklist item 3 asks a servicer/assignee whether it got the debt before or after 'default,' but the node never defines default (the FDCPA does not; courts look to the underlying contract or to charge-off/placement practice) and, more importantly, invites applying the (F)(iii) exclusion to a retained third-party collection agent. (F)(iii) shelters persons who 'obtained' the debt (ownership or servicing rights) not in default -- most courts do not use it to exempt a collection agency hired to work a delinquent account, and a dedicated collection agency is independently covered under the principal-purpose prong. As encoded, a user with a common early-out/pre-charge-off collector would likely be routed to 'excluded, no FDCPA claim,' a false negative on a live claim.
